cf.title: Fix recovery conflict canceling the startup progress timeout

input.subject: Fix recovery conflict canceling the startup progress timeout

verdict_reasoning: The problem is stated, reproduced on 15 through master by the reviewer, and the fix restores behaviour that log_startup_progress_interval already promises. The one surviving objection, prior-attempts-1, is a fixable design point. It asks how the lock and buffer-pin waits behave now that the progress timeout stays armed and can wake the startup process. A committer who knows the recovery-conflict code can settle it, and the backpatch to 15 needs the same person.

brief.title: Stop recovery conflicts from canceling the startup progress timeout
brief.problem: In archive recovery with hot_standby=on, one lock or buffer-pin recovery conflict stops "redo in progress" log messages for the rest of redo. Redo still finishes, but an admin watching a long PITR sees progress stop and may think recovery is stuck. The bug exists since 15, when STARTUP_PROGRESS_TIMEOUT was added.
brief.proposed_design: ResolveRecoveryConflictWithLock() and ResolveRecoveryConflictWithBufferPin() end with disable_all_timeouts(false), which also cancels STARTUP_PROGRESS_TIMEOUT. The patch makes each function disable only the two timeouts it enabled. The reviewer adds a TAP test in 031_recovery_conflict.pl with a gated Perl restore_command that holds replay around the conflicting record.
user_visible_surface: "redo in progress" messages under log_startup_progress_interval keep appearing after a lock or buffer-pin recovery conflict.
author_claims: One conflict cut progress messages from 22 to 7 in the author's reproduction; redo and data stay correct.
Only lock and buffer-pin conflicts are affected, because other conflict types do not wait on timeouts.
The fix is a backpatch candidate to 15; the reviewer reports v1 applies cleanly to 15 through master.
The reviewer reproduced the bug and confirmed the fix on 15 through master, and the v3 test passes on CI including Windows.
The v3 test adds about 3 seconds to 031 and does not depend on replay speed.
brief.thread_state: Only the reviewer, Ritesh Kumar, replied; he supports the fix, posted v3 with a test, and suggests backpatching the fix to 15 and the test to 17. No committer has commented, and the author moved the entry back to Needs review without saying why in the visible thread.
unclear: The thread does not say whether any other code in the startup process arms timeouts that the old disable_all_timeouts() call was silently clearing.
The thread does not say whether the old comment assuming no other outstanding timeouts is updated or removed.
The thread does not say how CF 7372, which reworks the same resolvers, will be reconciled if it lands first.
The thread does not say why the author changed the status from Ready for Committer back to Needs review.

prior_attempts.title: Revert "Get rid of the dedicated latch for signaling the startup process".
prior_attempts.quote: Because it broke the assumption that the startup process waiting for the recovery conflict on buffer pin should be waken up only by buffer unpin or the timeout enabled in ResolveRecoveryConflictWithBufferPin().
prior_attempts.reason:
Revert ac22929a26, as well as the followup fix 113d3591b8. Because it broke
the assumption that the startup process waiting for the recovery conflict
on buffer pin should be waken up only by buffer unpin or the timeout enabled
in ResolveRecoveryConflictWithBufferPin(). It caused, for example,
SIGHUP signal handler or walreceiver process to wake that startup process
up unnecessarily frequently.

Additionally, add the comments about why that dedicated latch that
the reverted patch tried to get rid of should not be removed.

Thanks to Kyotaro Horiguchi for the discussion.
prior_attempts.what_is_different: [P3] removed the startup process's dedicated latch. This patch changes which timeouts the resolvers cancel, but it leaves the progress timeout armed as a periodic wakeup source during the same buffer-pin wait.

objections.title: Progress timeout stays armed during conflict waits, which wake the startup process
objections.failure_scenario: An admin sets log_startup_progress_interval below deadlock_timeout during PITR with hot_standby=on. Each progress tick sets the latch, so the startup process wakes from its buffer-pin or lock wait and calls the resolver again. If the resolver re-arms STANDBY_DEADLOCK_TIMEOUT on each call, the deadlock check may never fire, and the wait lasts until max_standby_archive_delay, or forever at -1.
objections.argument: [P3] was reverted because it broke the assumption that a startup process waiting on a buffer-pin conflict is woken only by unpin or by the timeout that ResolveRecoveryConflictWithBufferPin() enabled. With this patch, STARTUP_PROGRESS_TIMEOUT stays armed through every conflict wait, which is the kind of extra wakeup [P3] warns about. Today this happens only during the first conflict; the patch makes it happen in all of them. Messages #1-#3 do not discuss wakeups during the wait.
objections.author_must_show: How do the lock and buffer-pin waits behave when the progress timeout fires repeatedly, for example with log_startup_progress_interval shorter than deadlock_timeout?

precedents.title: Revert "Get rid of the dedicated latch for signaling the startup process".

critic.reasoning: Any timeout firing sets the process latch, and both resolvers wait on that latch and re-arm STANDBY_DEADLOCK_TIMEOUT on each call, so the scenario is plausible. It needs log_startup_progress_interval below deadlock_timeout, which is not the default, and the thread does not discuss it.

Does any other startup-process code arm a timeout and rely on the old disable_all_timeouts() call to clear it?

committability.owner_note: Someone who knows the startup process's recovery-conflict waits and the timeout and latch code in standby.c would have to own it.
committability.liability: The owner signs for startup-process wait behaviour during lock and buffer-pin conflicts on six branches, 15 through master, and for a new TAP test with per-branch variants.
committability.author_follow_up: The author changed the CF status on 2026-11-03 but has not replied in the thread after message #1; the reviewer wrote and maintains the test.

priority.reason: The fix touches one file and narrows two cleanup calls, and the reviewer verified it on 15 through master with a test. It affects admins who run queries during archive recovery with hot_standby=on, and it needs one answer on wakeups during the wait.

provisional_note: Without the code, I could not check whether the resolvers re-arm STANDBY_DEADLOCK_TIMEOUT on each wakeup, whether the outdated comment is updated, or whether other startup-process timeouts relied on the old cleanup.

precedents_retrieved.title: timeout parameters in libpq
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patches add a tcp_user_timeout parameter on the server and in libpq that sets the Linux TCP_USER_TIMEOUT socket option. They also add a libpq socket_timeout parameter that closes the connection when a query result does not arrive in time.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Fabien COELHO's review asked why the server-side statement_timeout is not enough for socket_timeout. He also found that a timeout drops and resets the connection instead of cancelling the query, and that pqWait duplicates pqWaitTimed logic. The patch had no tests and no documentation. Andrei Yahorau warned that the pqWait change breaks callers that expect to wait forever; the author planned new patches after an absence, and the visible thread ends with the review.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: I'd like clarifications about the use case that needs this specific feature, especially to understand why the server-side "statement_timeout" setting is not right enough.

precedents_retrieved.title: Logical replication timeout
precedents_retrieved.summary: A walsender spent hours unlinking every possible spill file name for a large transaction in ReorderBufferRestoreCleanup, so the subscriber timed out and decoding restarted in a loop. The patch records which WAL segments a transaction actually spilled to, so cleanup removes only those files.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The visible messages do not show why. The last shown message, in March 2025, only reports a rebase. A reviewer had also asked for a second patch that sends progress updates during long loops such as cleanup, and no message shows that patch.

precedents_retrieved.title: socket_timeout in interfaces/libpq
precedents_retrieved.summary: Add a socket_timeout connection parameter to libpq so a client stops waiting and disconnects when a non-functional, overloaded server stops responding. The timeout was to be enforced inside pqWait(), the point where libpq clients can wait without end.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Michael Paquier said earlier reviewers did not like an option that forces a cancellation on the connection. He also objected that a timeout in pqWait() skips the cleanup that pqDropConnection() normally does, since pqWait() is written never to time out. Reviewers did not engage further, and David Steele returned the patch, which no longer applied and still had no consensus.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
Just with a quick look, assuming that you can bypass all
cleanup operations normally taken by pqDropConnection() through a
hijacking of pqWait() is not fine as this routine explicitely assumes
to *never* have a timeout for its wait.

precedents_retrieved.title: Microsecond-based timeouts
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch adds WaitLatchUs(), a latch wait with a timeout in microseconds, so code that sleeps to spread CPU or I/O can use high-resolution timers and still process other events. Only Linux 5.11+ (epoll_pwait2()), FreeBSD and macOS (kevent()) can wait less than 1 ms; other systems round up to milliseconds.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The visible messages do not show why. The author posted it as a proof of concept for a later cycle because the needed Linux syscall was too new. The only reply, from Andres Freund, discussed the choice of units and did not object to the idea.

precedents_retrieved.title: Generalize ereport_startup_progress infrastructure
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch moves the ereport_startup_progress infrastructure into elog.c/.h as a generic ereport_progress API, renames log_startup_progress_interval to log_progress_report_interval, and passes the interval to begin_progress_report_phase(). Follow-up patches would use it for postmaster removal of temp files and temp relation files, and later for checkpointer file processing.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Robert Haas said neither proposed use was the right way to solve its problem. The postmaster use changed timeout.c and relied on the timeout infrastructure, which he did not consider safe there. The checkpointer use needed more design work on how it interacts with log_checkpoints and the existing checkpoint logging. The author withdrew the entry about two weeks after his last message, which proposed new GUC designs and got no visible reply.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: At the same time, I don't think the overall picture here is too clear yet. I'm reluctant to commit to a specific UI for a feature whose scope we don't seem to know.

precedents_retrieved.title: hostorder and failover_timeout for libpq
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch adds two libpq connection parameters. `hostorder` (sequential or random) sets the order in which the hosts in a multi-host connection string are tried, and `failover_timeout` makes libpq loop over the hosts until one connects or the timeout expires.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The patch stopped applying, and the author did not rebase it or split it into separate `hostorder` and `failover_timeout` patches as Michael Paquier asked. Michael Paquier also doubted that a random mode alone justifies reworking libpq, and suggested that applications build their own connection strings. Tom Lane objected that the patch uses terms different from pgJDBC for nearly the same feature and overlaps two other patch threads, and these points were not addressed.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
As this hasn't been done, and Tom's questions haven't been addressed,
I'm marking this as returned with feedback.

precedents_retrieved.title: This adds a new GUC parameter that automatically rolls back prepared transactions that have remained unresolved beyond the configured timeout. The cleanup is performed by the checkpointer process.
precedents_retrieved.objectors: Andrey Borodin, Artur Zakirov, Greg Sabino Mullane
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch adds a GUC, prepared_orphaned_transaction_timeout, that makes the checkpointer roll back prepared transactions older than the timeout. It is disabled by default (0) and is modelled on idle_in_transaction_session_timeout and similar timeouts.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Reviewers said a silent rollback breaks the 2PC protocol: after all participants PREPARE, COMMIT must succeed on a healthy database, and only the transaction manager knows whether a dangling prepared transaction should be committed or rolled back. An orphaned prepared transaction signals a serious malfunction that needs monitoring, and a DBA who wants a timeout can use a cron job. Users who enable 2PC are expected to have their own monitoring and handling.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: Silent rollback in any scenario I can imagine is a disaster.

precedents_retrieved.title: Stmt timeout error can be sent after a CommandComplete
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch fixes a race where the statement timeout fires after the last message but before disable_statement_timeout, so a later CHECK_FOR_INTERRUPTS sends a statement timeout error after CommandComplete. It resets the timeout indicator through get_timeout_indicator when the timeout is no longer active.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Tom Lane pointed out that another pgsql-hackers thread already covers this area and that the timeout handling has more bugs than this one. The author agreed it is the same kind of issue and withdrew the entry to join that thread.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
I agree that this area is a bit buggy, but I think it's got more
problems than just this.

precedents_retrieved.title: Revert "Add redo LSN to pgstats files"
precedents_retrieved.summary:
Revert "Add redo LSN to pgstats files"
Reverted commit(s): Add redo LSN to pgstats files
precedents_retrieved.objection:
This reverts commit b860848232aa, that was added as a prerequisite for
the support of pgstats data flush across checkpoints, linking a pgstats
file to a specific checkpoint redo LSN.

As reported, this is proving to be currently problematic when going
through a pg_upgrade, that does direct manipulations of the control file
in the new cluster.  The LSN stored in the pgstats file is not able to
cope with any changes done in the control file by pg_upgrade yet,
causing the pgstats file to be discarded when starting the new cluster
after overriding its redo LSN (one is a `pg_resetwal -l` where the new
cluster's start LSN is bumped by a hardcoded value of 8 segments, see
copy_xact_xlog_xid).

The least painful path going forward is likely going to be a refactor of
the pgstats code so as it is possible to read and write some of its data
with some routines in src/common/, so as pg_upgrade or pg_resetwal are
able to update its data.  The main point is that we are going to need a
LSN in the stats file should we make it written at checkpoint time and
not only as part of a shutdown sequence.  It is too late to dive into
these details for v18, so let's revert the change, and let's try to
figure out all the details in the next release cycle.  The pgstats file
is currently only written as part of a shutdown sequence, and its
contents are still lost on crash, same as older releases.

Bump PGSTAT_FILE_FORMAT_ID.

roaster_notes.note: No earlier attempt at this fix is in the precedent list. Message #3 points to CF 7372 and CF 6876 as related work in the same area, but neither is a rejected attempt at this fix.

The fix adds no syntax, GUC, catalog object, psql behaviour or dump state. The only user-visible change is that "redo in progress" messages under log_startup_progress_interval keep appearing after a lock or buffer-pin conflict, which the setting already promises, so back branches change only by restoring the documented behaviour. [P3] concerns startup-process wakeups, which is outside this angle.

The patch adds no persistent or cross-node state and changes no on-disk format, WAL record, catalog, wire protocol or exported API, so it is safe to backpatch from this angle. It narrows which in-process timeouts the startup process clears after a lock or buffer-pin conflict on a hot standby. [P3] concerns startup-process wakeups during conflict waits, which this patch does not change.

The patch only changes which startup-process timeouts the lock and buffer-pin conflict resolvers disable, so it has no privilege or exposure aspect. It adds no new privilege, view, message content or user-controlled input. A read-only standby user could already trigger these conflicts, and after the fix they no longer silence progress logging.

I have no maintenance or fit objection. The patch narrows cleanup in two functions to the timeouts they enable, adds no hot-path cost and fits normal timeout practice; the v3 test fails loudly if CF 7372 restores disable_all_timeouts(). Without the code I could not check whether the outdated comment is updated, or whether any other startup-process timeout relied on the old blanket cancel. [P3] concerns latch wakeups and does not apply.

This is a bug fix for a timeout that existing code cancels by mistake. No existing feature, setting or extension restores "redo in progress" messages after a lock or buffer-pin conflict, and CF 6876 covers standby-mode replay, not archive recovery. The fix narrows existing disable_timeout() use and adds no second mechanism.

No demand objection. This fixes a bug in an existing feature, log_startup_progress_interval, so it restores documented behaviour and needs no new users. The cost is a narrower timeout cleanup in two resolvers, with no new UI, GUC or hot-path work, and the reviewer reproduced the bug on 15 through master (messages #1 and #2).
